observations: She turns its pages beside her father and enjoys animal pictures.
She takes the book to show mother and grandmother.
Narrator compares royal possession/riding with her pleasure in pictures.
Grandmother responds impatiently; alphabet teaching follows.
interpretation: Pleasure precedes formal reading in this narrated encounter.
Showing the pictures to others makes her excitement active and social.
This offers a precise literary companion to the author’s children-and-books question, not proof about modern children or media outcomes.
suggested_passage: A few paragraphs later, Rebati receives a primer. Before her lessons begin, she turns its pages beside her father, delighted by pictures of elephants, horses and cattle. She runs to show them to her mother and then her grandmother. The narrator pauses over that small pleasure: kings possess elephants and horses; others enjoy riding them; Rebi is happy simply to see their pictures. Her grandmother’s impatient response makes the contrast sharper. The book is already something Rebati wants to share, before she can read it. Follow that movement—from looking, to delight, to showing someone else—and the question of bringing a child towards books becomes a particular child’s experience, rather than an adult instruction.
